title: What is multi-catch, how does catch (IOException | SQLException e) differ from separate catches?
shortTitle: Multi-catch (Java 7+) — catch (A | B e), implicitly final, no parent-child

s1_definition.profdef: Multi-catch (Java 7) combines multiple exception types in ONE catch block: `catch (IOException | SQLException e)`. The variable `e` is implicitly FINAL (cannot reassign). The types must be UNRELATED — `catch (IOException | FileNotFoundException e)` is a compile error because FileNotFoundException IS-A IOException (parent-child). Benefits: eliminates duplicate code across separate catch blocks. The compiled bytecode is more efficient than separate catches with identical bodies.
s1_definition.oneliner: `catch (A | B e)` = one block, multiple unrelated types. Variable is final. No parent-child pairs. Eliminates duplicate catch bodies.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Multi-catch (Java 7) combines multiple exception types in ONE catch block: `catch (IOException | SQLException e)`. The variable `e` is implicitly FINAL (cannot reassign). The types must be UNRELATED — `catch (IOException | FileNotFoundException e)` is a compile error because FileNotFoundException IS-A IOException (parent-child). Benefits: eliminates duplicate code across separate catch blocks. The compiled bytecode is more efficient than separate catches with identical bodies.

**One line to remember:** `catch (A | B e)` = one block, multiple unrelated types. Variable is final. No parent-child pairs. Eliminates duplicate catch bodies.

sections.s3_banking: Problem — the account statement export reads a PDF template from a file and loads ledger rows from the database. Reading the file can throw an IOException and loading the ledger can throw a SQLException, but in both cases the service does exactly the same thing: log the failure and wrap it in an ExportException. Writing two separate catch blocks meant copy-pasting the same two lines, and when the log message was updated, one copy was missed and the two branches drifted apart. Fix: a single `catch (IOException | SQLException e)` multi-catch block handles both unrelated exception types with one body, so there is one place to maintain and no chance of drift. This mini-project builds the export method and a JUnit test that forces each exception type and confirms both are handled by the same block.
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three export requests — one that triggers an IOException, one that triggers a SQLException, and one that succeeds.

**Step 1.** The IOException request enters `export("io")`. Reading the template file fails and throws IOException. The multi-catch `catch (IOException | SQLException e)` matches the first listed type and runs its single shared body, logging and wrapping the error.

**Step 2.** The SQLException request enters `export("sql")`. The file read succeeds but the ledger query throws SQLException. The SAME multi-catch block matches the second listed type and runs the identical body — no duplicated code, no risk of the two branches drifting apart.

**Step 3.** Inside the block, the variable `e` is implicitly final. Any attempt to reassign it (for example `e = new IOException(...)`) would be a compile error, which keeps the handler type-safe when the concrete type is unknown.

**Step 4.** The happy-path request `export("SAV2001")` throws nothing, so the catch block is skipped entirely and the method returns the exported value. The test verifies both exception types land in the multi-catch and the success path bypasses it.

```
INFO    2026-10-22T21:06:55 StatementExport SAV2001 -> EXPORTED
WARNING 2026-10-22T21:06:55 StatementExport io  -> MULTI_CATCH IOException template missing
WARNING 2026-10-22T21:06:55 StatementExport sql -> MULTI_CATCH SQLException ledger query failed
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ MULTI-CATCH: ONE BLOCK, MULTIPLE TYPES ═══

  try {
      fileStore.read(acctId);   ── may throw IOException ──┐
      ledger.load(acctId);      ── may throw SQLException ─┤
  }                                                        │
                                                           ▼
  catch (IOException | SQLException e)   ← SINGLE handler, e is FINAL
      │  log.error("export failed", e)
      │  throw new ExportException("export failed", e)
      ▼
  Caller receives ExportException (cause preserved)

  ═══ LEGAL vs ILLEGAL COMBINATIONS ═══

  LEGAL  : catch (IOException | SQLException e)      ← unrelated siblings
  ILLEGAL: catch (IOException | FileNotFoundException e)  ← parent-child
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  StatementExportService.export(acctId)
       │
       try { readFile(); queryDb(); }
       │
       ├─ catch (IOException | SQLException e)   ← ONE block, TWO types
       │       log + wrap in ExportException     (identical handling)
       │
       └─ types must be UNRELATED (not parent-child)
  Multi-catch avoids duplicated catch bodies.
  Variable e is implicitly FINAL — cannot reassign.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Multi-catch `catch (A | B e)` handles multiple unrelated exception types in one block. The variable is implicitly final (can't reassign — unlike separate catches). Types must NOT have parent-child relationship. Use when separate catches would have identical bodies, so there is a single body to maintain and no risk of the branches drifting apart.
